title: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar
hook: an Upanishad's graduation speech, and a second text that says: go the very day it calls
carry: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar
tomorrow: why does an old graduation start with a bath?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the whole five years in seven sits with a hymn that asks who really knows. Today the path turns to what comes after study: the graduate's path.

Graduation speeches have a formula: follow your dreams, the world is yours, don't forget us. The Taittiriya Upanishad has a graduation speech of its own, from a teacher to the student who is leaving, and it sounds nothing like that. It's a short list of plain instructions. And another Upanishad, the Jabala, gives a very different send-off. Two voices, both inside the tradition. Let them talk.
screen: `FOLLOW YOUR DREAMS.` → `A TEACHER'S PARTING LIST.` → `A SECOND VOICE.`

segments.voice: First voice, the Taittiriya. Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the student. Speak the truth. Practice dharma. Don't neglect your study. Bring the teacher a gift, and don't cut off the line of your family. Don't neglect your well-being, or what helps you thrive. Give with faith, give with modesty. And if you're ever unsure what to do, act the way the thoughtful, gentle people near you who love dharma would act. Its best case: the world is where the learning gets used. A home, a family, work, gifts: that's the classroom now. Second voice, the Jabala. It lays out the familiar order, student, then householder, then forest dweller, then sannyasa, the life of one who has laid everything down. Then it adds: or one may go forth straight from student life, or from the house, or from the forest. The very day the pull to let go arrives, that day, go. Its best case: when the call comes, waiting can be its own way of saying no. Notice what neither does. The Taittiriya doesn't call leaving wrong; the Jabala doesn't call the household small. And the first voice even names how to decide: look at the wise, gentle people around you. That's the seminar after graduation.
screen: `SPEAK THE TRUTH. PRACTICE DHARMA.` · `IN DOUBT, ASK THE GENTLE WISE.` · `THE JABALA: GO THE DAY IT CALLS.` · `NEITHER CALLS THE OTHER SMALL.`

segments.voice: Name one wish for the next year of your life, in a few words. Then name the obstacle most likely to get in its way, the one inside you. Then a plan: if that obstacle shows up, I will do this. Hold the three, wish, obstacle, plan, with the breath.
The graduate's path: what comes after study. In the Taittiriya, a life in the world; in the Jabala, going forth the day it calls.
Your line: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar. When unsure, look to the gentle and the wise. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Taittiriya's parting instruction (1.11) is still recited at some Indian school and university graduations; the Jabala Upanishad is one of the texts that later renunciant orders cite for leaving home.

chat.says: Dad: college, job, THEN 'the spiritual stuff.' but Nani's cousin went to an ashram at 19. who's right??
options: the texts hold both: one teacher's send-off says live in the world; the Jabala says go the day it calls.
Dad. the texts say leaving the world is only for old people, once everything else is done.
Nani's cousin. the texts say the world is a trap, so the sooner you leave it the better.
chat.meaning: The Taittiriya sends the graduate into the world; the Jabala allows going forth from any stage, the day the pull comes. Neither calls the other small.

Taittiriya.meaning: an Upanishad with a teacher's parting words to a graduate

Jabala.meaning: an Upanishad that allows renouncing the world from any stage

dharma.meaning: right order, duty, the way things ought to go

sannyasa.meaning: renunciation: the life of one who has laid everything down

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1–4 (having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: speak truth, practice dharma, do not neglect study; bring the teacher a gift, do not cut off the line of offspring; do not neglect welfare and prosperity; give with faith, with modesty; in doubt about conduct, act as thoughtful, devoted, gentle brahmins who love dharma would act)

Jabala Upanishad 4 (having completed studenthood, become a householder; then a forest dweller; then go forth; or else go forth from studenthood, from the house or from the forest; the very day one becomes dispassionate, that very day go forth)

notes: Block 'the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar', day 1 of 3 (1781–1783). The voice reads 'a Keeper seminar' as the old advice to learn from the wise and gentle around you; it never names or implies a specific Keeper.
Debate shape: two real views inside the tradition, each given its best case; neither ranked. The fork asks the learner to state the other side's best case.
